intro: Two kinds of writing sit at the heart of the Tanakh, and this unit reads both up close. The first is law: the ten sayings and the case laws of Exodus 19–24. The Torah says they were given at a mountain in the wilderness and sealed as a covenant between God and Israel. The second is prophecy: the speeches of Amos, Hosea, Micah and Isaiah. They told a people keeping the rituals that God wanted justice, loyal love and return. The prophets quote the law, and the law already sounds like the prophets. Both protect the stranger, the widow and the orphan.

We read these texts as a public school studies them: as Jewish tradition reads them, as historians and literary scholars read them, and in comparison with the world around them. Hammurabi's laws sit beside the goring ox of Exodus. Hittite treaties sit beside the Sinai scene. Rashi, Ibn Ezra, the Talmud and Maimonides sit beside modern scholars. Martin Luther King Jr. and Abraham Joshua Heschel sit beside Amos. We describe what each says and how each has been read, and we do not decide whether any of it is true.

By the end you will be able to do several things. You will explain why the same ten sayings are numbered three different ways. You will compare an ancient Babylonian law with one in Exodus and say what changed. You will state how the rabbis read "eye for eye." You will read Amos 5, Micah 6 and Isaiah 58 closely enough to say who is speaking to whom and what is demanded. You will explain why Jonah is read on Yom Kippur afternoon. And you will learn how these texts moved from the synagogue's weekly reading into the streets of Selma and Chicago.
bigQuestion: How do the Torah's covenant laws and the prophets' demands for justice belong to one conversation, and how have their readers carried it on?

timeline.t: Laws of Ur-Nammu, the oldest known law collection, written in Sumerian
Hammurabi's laws carved on a stone pillar in Babylon
Hittite kings begin making treaties in the form scholars compare to Sinai
The Torah's Sinai scene: ten sayings, the Covenant Code and the sealing of the covenant
Amos of Tekoa preaches at Bethel in the northern kingdom
Hosea prophesies in the north; Micah and Isaiah begin in Judah soon after
Assyria destroys the northern kingdom and its capital Samaria
Babylon destroys Jerusalem and the First Temple; exile begins
"Comfort ye": Isaiah 40–55, which most scholars date to the exile, names Cyrus of Persia
The Talmud reads "eye for eye" as compensation and sets the haftarot of warning and comfort
French excavators find Hammurabi's stone at Susa
King quotes Amos in Washington; Heschel marches with him from Selma

words.d: brit in Hebrew; a binding bond with duties on each side; in the Torah, the bond between God and Israel sealed at Sinai
an ancient pact between a great king and a vassal, with a prologue of past favors, duties, witnesses, blessings and curses
the ten sayings of Exodus 20 and Deuteronomy 5; the Torah calls them "the ten words"
the scholarly name for the case laws of Exodus 21–23, read aloud and sealed in Exodus 24
king of Babylon, c. 1750 BCE, whose 282 laws survive on a stone pillar now in the Louvre
"eye for eye"; the law of matching retaliation, which rabbinic tradition reads as monetary compensation
the stranger or resident foreigner whom the Torah protects, "for ye were strangers in the land of Egypt"
the feast of weeks, seven weeks after Passover; a harvest festival that Jewish tradition links to the giving of the Torah
justice and righteousness, the pair of words the prophets demand, as in Amos 5:24
loyal love or faithful kindness; what Hosea 6:6 and Micah 6:8 value above sacrifice
the reading from the Prophets that follows the Torah reading in synagogue on Shabbat and festivals
return or repentance, from shuv, to turn; the prophets' demand and the theme of the Days of Awe

test.q: In the Sinai scene, what comes between God's offer (Exodus 19:5–6) and the ten sayings (Exodus 20)?
choices: The people's consent: "All that the LORD hath spoken we will do"
test.why: Exodus 19:8 records the people's answer before the thunder and the sayings.

test.q: Which part of a Hittite suzerainty treaty does "who brought thee out of the land of Egypt" resemble?
choices: The prologue recalling the great king's past favors
The order to read the treaty aloud
test.why: The historical prologue recalls what the great king has done for the vassal, as Exodus 20:2 does.

test.q: What does the Torah itself call the ten sayings in Exodus 34:28 and Deuteronomy 4:13?
test.why: The Hebrew phrase is aseret hadevarim, "the ten words."

test.q: Which tradition counts "I am the LORD thy God" as the first of the ten?
test.why: The Jewish count begins with the statement of Exodus 20:2; the Christian counts treat it as a preface.

test.q: What is the biggest difference between Exodus 21:28–32 and Hammurabi 250–252 on the goring ox?
choices: Exodus stones the ox and treats the death as more than a payment; Hammurabi only sets a sum of silver
Hammurabi stones the ox; Exodus does not
Hammurabi has no law about oxen
test.why: Both blame the negligent owner, but only Exodus punishes the animal and puts the owner's life at stake.

test.q: How does the Talmud (Bava Kamma 83b–84a) read "eye for eye"?
choices: As monetary compensation for the injury
As a law only for slaves
As a law only for kings
test.why: Rabbinic tradition reads the verse as payment, listing five kinds of damages.

test.q: What reason does Exodus 22:20 give for not wronging the stranger?
choices: Because Israel was a stranger in Egypt
test.why: The verse grounds the law in memory: "for ye were strangers in the land of Egypt."

test.q: Which statement about Shavuot is a rabbinic teaching rather than a statement in the Torah's text?
choices: It comes seven weeks after Passover
It is the anniversary of the giving of the Torah
test.why: The Torah presents Shavuot as a harvest feast; the Sinai link comes from rabbinic calculation.

test.q: Who was Amos, and where did he preach?
choices: A herdsman from Tekoa in Judah who preached at Bethel in the northern kingdom
A priest of Bethel who preached in Jerusalem
A king of Israel who preached in Samaria
A scribe in Babylon who preached to the exiles
test.why: Amos 1:1 and Amos 7 give his origin and the scene at Bethel.

test.q: Which pair of Hebrew words does Amos 5:24 demand instead of festivals and songs?
test.why: Amos calls for justice (mishpat) and righteousness (tzedakah) to flow like water.

test.q: What did Yochanan ben Zakkai teach with Hosea 6:6 after the Temple fell?
choices: That sacrifice must be restored at once
That acts of loving-kindness atone as the Temple did
test.why: Avot de-Rabbi Natan 4 records his answer that chesed atones, citing "I desire mercy, and not sacrifice."

test.q: What does Micah 6:8 say the LORD requires?
choices: To do justly, love mercy and walk humbly with God
test.why: Micah 6:8 answers the escalating list of offerings with three verbs and the word "only."

test.q: Which Isaiah chapter is read on Yom Kippur morning, and what does it say about fasting?
choices: Isaiah 58: the fast God chooses is to free the oppressed and feed the hungry
Isaiah 1: your hands are full of blood
test.why: Isaiah 58 is the Yom Kippur morning haftarah and redefines the fast as care for others.

test.q: Why is Isaiah 40 read on the Shabbat after Tisha B'Av?
choices: Because it describes the destruction of the Temple
Because it opens seven weeks of comfort after the fast of mourning
Because it is the shortest chapter
test.why: Shabbat Nachamu begins the seven haftarot of consolation with "Comfort ye, comfort ye My people."

test.q: Why is the book of Jonah read on Yom Kippur afternoon?
choices: Because it describes the Temple service
Because an enemy city's turning from evil is held up as true teshuvah, and God's mercy is its theme
Because it is read on every fast day
test.why: Nineveh's repentance, praised in Mishnah Ta'anit 2:1, makes Jonah the model reading before the fast ends.

write.prompt: Amos, Hosea, Micah and Isaiah all say that worship without justice is unacceptable. Are they rejecting ritual, or demanding something of it? Argue from the text: cite Amos 5:21–24, Hosea 6:6 and one of Isaiah 1:11–17 or Isaiah 58:5–7, say what each passage says in its own context, and explain how at least two later readers (the Talmud, Avot de-Rabbi Natan, Ibn Ezra, Heschel, King) have read them.
tips: Name the book, chapter and verse for every passage you cite.
Attribute every reading: "the rabbis of the Talmud read this as…", "Heschel argued…", "most scholars hold…"
Quote from JPS 1917 and say so; paraphrase everything else in your own words.
Compare the readers rather than judging which one is right.
Use the unit's words: mishpat, tzedakah, chesed, teshuvah, haftarah.
